source.title: Neurons Speak in Ranges: Breaking Free from Discrete Neuronal Attribution
source.authors: Muhammad Umair Haider; Hammad Rizwan; Hassan Sajjad; Peizhong Ju; A. Siddique

page_placements.theme: Residual-stream and embedding basis dimensions (not MLP neurons) mix concepts

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures cross-concept overlap in salient language-model neurons and analyzes concept-conditioned activations using distributional and range-based methods, rather than reproducing the original vision-neuron analysis.
record.gate_note: Included results on salient-neuron overlap, activation-range patterns, and auxiliary-concept effects of neuron masking. The paper also reports MMLU, perplexity, and intervention-method results, but those are not separate evidence that neurons represent multiple concepts. Figure 2 values not stated in text are retained as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study's own analysis bears on V7. Neurons it calls polysemantic (salient for more than one class) show concept-specific activation ranges. Whether a neuron looks mixed therefore depends on which part of its range is examined. Its 'neurons' are hidden-state (residual-stream) dimensions at the CLS or last token, not MLP neurons. The concepts are coarse topic, sentiment or emotion class labels, so its overlap and masking results do not match V2's construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors treat a neuron as polysemantic if it is salient for more than one class. They conclude that such neurons still show concept-conditioned, Gaussian-like activation ranges with limited overlap, so range-based attribution and masking target concepts with less collateral damage. They acknowledge that concept ranges still partially overlap.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes labeled language-model activations, salient-neuron overlap, concept-conditioned distributions, and range-gated interventions; it does not reproduce the original image-neuron analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported dependence on model and dataset, GPT-2 layer, neuron saliency/ranking selection, and activation-range width τ. Early GPT-2 layers show more concept overlap; separation increases in deeper layers. Varying τ changes target and auxiliary performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Over 60% of the top-30% salient hidden-state dimensions in GPT-2 are shared between the two IMDB classes. Overlap is shown for other datasets by class count (Fig. 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dimensions of the residual stream ranked salient by mean |activation| are shared across task class labels.

fits_no_version.finding: Class-conditioned activation distributions overlap in early GPT-2 layers and separate from layers 5–6 onward.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Class separability of residual-stream dimensions increases with depth.

fits_no_version.finding: AUROC-based pairwise distributional overlap of concept-conditioned activations. Low for BERT; high for Llama (Emotions: 41.74% of pairs above 75%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept-conditioned activation ranges of hidden-state dimensions are separable to a degree that varies by model and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing 30–50% of salient penultimate-layer dimensions for one class reduces accuracy on other classes. The drop is large for Llama and near zero for BERT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ablating class-salient hidden-state dimensions causes collateral damage to other classes.

record.problems: The operational polysemanticity measure is overlap among top salient neurons across labeled classes, not a direct rate of neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts. The paper reports limited model and dataset comparisons, some findings are qualitative or figure-only, and the reported class concepts do not establish that the mixed inputs are unrelated.

untested.parts: MLP neurons are never analysed; only CLS or last-token hidden-state (residual-stream) dimensions. Concepts are related class labels, not unrelated tokens or contexts. No share of polysemantic neurons per layer is reported.
Initialization as a cause is cited (Lecomte et al.), not tested.
BERT, GPT-2 and Llama differ in training regime and setup at once. No controlled variation of activation function, architecture or regularization, and no reduction in the polysemantic share.
No test of whether apparent mixtures share one underlying feature.
Explanation-scoring methods are not compared. Saliency threshold is not varied for the polysemanticity count.

missing.what: Range separability of GPT-2 neurons salient for all classes. Neuron 480 is partially separable, neuron 675 fully overlapping, and 7–11 neurons are shown as box plots across DBPedia classes.
Correct description of Table 5 as AUROC distributional overlap (App. D.2), replacing salient-neuron overlap.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V2 and V5 links were removed. The 'neurons' here are residual-stream or CLS/last-token hidden-state components, not MLP neurons, and the concepts are related class labels. The V5 label cited rows not linked to V5, and model-family differences are confounded by training regime (fine-tuned vs few-shot). Masking comparator rows are the study's own method versus baseline. Table 5 was misread by the extractor. The SAE result (App. N) concerns SAE features, not neurons.

versions.untested_parts: The study analyzes language models, not image classifiers or InceptionV1.
The study uses labeled classification concepts and salient-neuron overlap, not unrelated-token response rates across transformer MLP neurons generally.
The study discusses superposition but does not manipulate feature capacity or test it as the cause of polysemanticity.
Initialization-related polysemanticity is cited from prior work; this study does not vary initialization, regularization, or training noise while controlling capacity.

It compares model families and reports different overlap statistics, but does not isolate activation function, architecture, or regularization effects, nor measure a reduction in the share of polysemantic neurons.
It does not determine whether canonical unrelated mixtures share a common feature or whether such mixtures are rare.
It varies saliency selection, layer, and activation-range width, but does not compare explanation-scoring methods.

relation.reason: Its own analysis bears on whether a polysemantic neuron looks mixed depending on the activation range examined.

tranche.reason: The study uses a different method (concept-conditioned activation distributions plus LLM-judged boundary samples) on V7's question, and its main results support V7. It argues against discrete whole-neuron attribution, which is V7's own restatement, not that V7 is wrong. Neuron 675 is only a side limitation. The test_reason gives only the supportive reading, and the reader also chose T2.

source_check.notes: The 'neurons' are hidden-state (residual-stream) components of the last token at the class-label position (App. H), mainly at the penultimate layer (Section 5.3, Limitations). 'Polysemantic' means salient for more than one class label, not unrelated contexts. GPT-2 is fine-tuned. Llama-3.2-3B is few-shot, with 2000 correctly predicted samples per class. The Llama V7 evidence is two hand-picked neurons, summarised by an LLM judge.

statements.problem: The parts about this study match the text: Llama-3.2-3B, AG-News, last-token output (App. H), neurons 1525/2587, mean vs boundary samples, Gemini Pro judge, 10 examples per point. The general lead ('monosemantic on top activations') does not describe this study exactly, because its upper-boundary samples also mix classes. The study-specific clause is accurate.

Neuron 675 is in fine-tuned GPT-2 on AG-News. It is salient for all classes at the 5% threshold and has completely overlapping activations (App. D.1, Fig. 6). Limitations says concept distributions still partially overlap. Matches.
The authors are not the original's group. The Llama activation-range dependence is fair for this study: qualitative, two neurons.
Section 3: for two-class IMDB, overlap of top-30% salient neurons (hidden-state components) in GPT-2 is more than 60%. Matches.
